title: Eiffel Excellence Scholarship 2027: €1,181 a Month and the Nomination Game

intro: France’s Eiffel scholarship cannot be applied for directly — institutions nominate. Amounts, age limits, deadlines and the nomination strategy for 2027.
description: Eiffel Excellence Scholarship 2027: allowance rates, age limits, fields and the institution nomination process.
author: NextApply Team
excerpt: Eiffel 2027: €1,181/month master’s, €1,700 PhD — and the institution nomination rule that decides everything.
content:
The France Excellence Eiffel scholarship is France’s elite attraction programme for future foreign decision-makers — and it runs on a rule that surprises almost everyone: you cannot apply directly. The French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs funds it, Campus France administers it, but only a French institution can nominate you. The 2027 call opened on 1 October 2026, institutions set their own internal deadlines through November and December, and Campus France accepts institution-uploaded applications until 8 January 2027. If you are reading this in autumn, your real deadline is the internal one — often mid-November.

What the scholarship pays

Eiffel laureates receive a monthly allowance of €1,200 at master’s level and €2,100 at doctoral level — rates that rose from €1,181 and €1,700 with effect from January 2026, plus international return travel, health insurance, and cultural activities — with housing assistance where available. The allowance does not itself pay tuition, but French public universities routinely enrol Eiffel laureates without tuition fees, and the ministries behind the programme expect host institutions to cover the remainder of costs. Think of the package as salary-plus: enough to live respectably in Paris, comfortably anywhere else in France.

Eligibility has an age ceiling that disqualifies more applicants than grades do: 25 or under at master’s level and 30 or under at doctoral level in the year of the call. Non-French nationals only — and candidates previously rejected by an Eiffel application at the same level can be re-presented only once.

The seven fields

Eiffel funds two broad axes. The sciences cover biology and health, ecological transition, mathematics and digital sciences, and engineering sciences. The humanities and social sciences cover history, French language and civilisation; law and political science; and economics and management. Your target programme must sit inside one of these areas — checking that before anything else saves weeks.

How the nomination game works

  1. Choose institutions, not the scholarship. Shortlist French master’s or PhD programmes inside the seven fields; each sets its own Eiffel calendar (many close internally by mid-November).
  2. Build the case for the institution. Universities nominate a limited number of candidates — your CV, grades, and a research or career project that makes the institution want to spend one of its slots on you.
  3. The institution submits. If nominated, the university uploads your file to Campus France by 8 January 2027. Results arrive around April; laureates start the following academic year.

Because institutions weigh Eiffel candidates for prestige as well as merit, your application is really a marketing document for the university’s own international strategy — show them what your name does for their profile.

The Eiffel CV is a format, not a freeform document

Campus France requires nominations on a standardised CV template — sections for education, work experience, distinctions, language skills and the candidate’s project, in that order, with no other layout accepted. The constraint is a gift if you use it: the template forces institutions to compare like with like, and candidates who write the "project" section as a career narrative tied to France — what the degree unlocks, where you intend to work, what cooperation with France continues afterwards — consistently outperform applicants with stronger grades and a generic file. Attach the template early; leave the freeform CV for the institution’s own admissions file.

If the first attempt fails, remember the re-presentation rule: an institution may re-present a rejected candidate once at the same level. A stronger second file — new research output, a sharper project — occasionally flips the result, which is why staying on good terms with your Eiffel coordinator matters even in a rejection year.

Strategy notes

  • Email the international office, not just admissions. The Eiffel coordinator at each institution can tell you their internal deadline and how many nominations they typically make.
  • Masters beat PhDs on odds. The master’s cohort is larger, and France treats the programme as a talent pipeline — a master’s Eiffel often leads to a funded doctoral track afterwards.
  • Pair with parallel applications. Eiffel results (April) land after Erasmus Mundus deadlines — our EMJM calendar and the 12-month timeline show how to sequence both without duplicating work.
